Let's look at your garden hose.

On one end, you have a water pump. Next, you have a garden hose. Finally, you have an empty bucket.

In this case, electrons are like the water. See, we know that the tendency of matter is to move from an ordered state to a disordered state - in a process known as increasing entropy. This stems from the 2nd Law of Thermodynamics.

Let's turn the water on, shall we? Now, the water is going to move through the pipe - it's going to be the current. (Amps.) If you increase the pressure, water can still only move so fast through the hose. If you make the hose larger, you'll have less water pressure if you're still pumping the same amount of water.

Here, it gets complicated.

You're electricity is moving through copper wire. This wire is made up of atoms. These atoms do, technically, move - but for this moment in time we're just going to consider them stationary.

What's happening is the power source (the electric company) is putting charged electrons into the system. These charged electrons seek to become disordered - they move (like water) to the lowest possible state (water seeks its own level and electrons seek a balance). Every atom has one of three types of particles. They are positive protons, neutral neutrons, and negative electrons.

Just like the water pump makes the water want to come out the other end of the hose, so to do electrons work. See, what's actually happening is the atoms of copper (our conductor for this journey) don't really move enough to matter. (They do technically move - all matter loves to dance - but that's irrelevant.)

What's happening, when you turn on the switch, is the atoms of copper start exchanging electrons. The electrons move from one atom to the other, as they seek equilibrium. They work their way to a least ordered state, from hot to cold, or increasing in entropy - it's what they do. Entropy is the final boss of the universe, but I digress.

This is actually a pretty slow process. But, see, the atoms of copper already had electrons. They just didn't have electrons in number as high as what's being added.

Now, imagine the copper wire is like the above mentioned garden hose. A larger hose will allow more water to move through it. A smaller hose will let less water through it - but will have greater water pressure (assuming the pump is the same size). In this case, the copper wire's size matters, as does the proximity of atoms to one another.

Electron A is an excess electron associated with atom A, so it passes it off to atom B. Atom B has now got an extra electron and A doesn't want it back, as atom A already has a new one as the power company added more to the system. So, it passes that charged electron down to atom C - and it keeps going like that.

Now, some atoms are stingy. They've held onto their electrons and they're not going to give them up right now. That's okay - the electron will find another atom to give it's spare electron to. The more atoms there are, the greater the volume of electrons can be. However, the greater the volume is, the more chances it has of finding an atom that just doesn't want to swap an electron.
